about.me_text: Nobody appointed you to anything. You have no title, and there is nothing stopping anyone else in the village from doing exactly what you do. You are simply the one everybody comes to when something gets stuck — and that lasts only as long as they keep coming.
about.name_prompt: What would you like to call this village?
about.title: The village, before you step in
about.village_text: A small village, with no wall and no gate. Six groups live here — except one, which only passes through — and each of them is bothered by something different.

amend.empty_book: There's not a single rule in the book. You wrote none, so there's nothing to change now — and that was a choice too, at every moment when you could have written one.
amend.heading: Changing What's Already Written
amend.intro: This is the rule. You wrote it, and since then it's been in the book like everything else.
amend.rule_says: And what you wrote about changing rules says:

decide.collision_first_time_note: Sometimes you can see ahead of time that a new rule clashes with an old one. Sometimes you only find out once it has already happened to someone.
decide.collision_intro: Two rules you wrote apply here, and they say opposite things.
decide.no_rule_intro: There is nothing in the book that touches this. Nobody wrote a rule for it at the time.
decide.other_decides_intro: There's a rule in the book that covers this. You wrote it, and somebody else applies it now.
decide.rule_applies_intro: There is a rule in the book that covers this. You wrote it.
decide.write_rule_intro: There is no rule that touches this. You can write one now — and it will stay in the book.

opener.comes_but: It took a while before {group} came, and they told you only part of it.
opener.comes_to_you: You heard it from {group} first, and they told you everything.
opener.stops_coming: Nobody from {group} came to tell you. You heard about it later, from someone else.

app.override_note: Someone says it out loud, without raising their voice: “So the rules here are whatever you decide at the moment?”
app.title: First Rule

most_senior.label: Whoever has been here longest decides
most_senior.template: whoever has been here longest decides

two_together.label: Two together
two_together.template: you and whoever has been here longest decide together

authority.intro: There is no line in the book that says who decides. As long as there isn't, anyone who decides something is exactly as right as anyone else. You can write that line now — and it will apply to you too.
authority.sentence: In this village: {form}. This applies to {who}.
authority.who_note: If you choose “the village chooses,” this field also decides who votes.

builder.clash_intro: This cannot live alongside a rule you have already written:
builder.clash_note: You can write it anyway. Both rules will stay in the book, and someone will have to decide which one holds.

help_victim.label: Must help the one who was hurt, one day
help_victim.template: they have to help the one who was hurt, one day

lose_next_turn.label: Loses the right to it next time
lose_next_turn.template: they lose the right to it next time

return_or_fix.label: Must give it back or fix it
return_or_fix.template: they have to give it back or fix it

village_decides.label: The village decides case by case
village_decides.template: the village decides case by case

builder.skip: Do not write a rule this time
builder.subject_prefix: The rule you are writing, about {subject}

when_harmed.label: Only if someone is hurt by it
when_harmed.template: only if someone is hurt by it

when_scarce.label: Only when there is not enough for everyone
when_scarce.template: only when there is not enough for everyone

anyone_present.label: Anyone who is here right now
anyone_present.template: Anyone who is here right now

c1s1.lesson: Until now there was no rule here, so there was nothing to break either. The moment you wrote one, the village has something it can point at — and that works in both directions.
c1s1.no_rule_outcome: You decided nothing. Dana walks off with the bucket, Yotam stays by the well. The next morning he rolls a large stone over it.

outcomes.ask_first: Dana brings the bucket back and asks. Yotam nods, a little surprised that anyone asked him at all. That evening he tells two other people that something here got settled.
outcomes.by_turn: You set an order: Yotam first, then the herd. It works. It takes everyone longer, and nobody is left without.
outcomes.forbidden: Dana empties the bucket back into the well and leads the herd away. In the afternoon she was seen looking for water in the dry riverbed, far off.
outcomes.share_equally: The well is open to everyone equally. Dana fills without asking, and two more after her. Yotam stands to one side, looking at the well he dug.

c1s1.override_outcome: You decided differently from what is written in your own book. Yotam looks at you and says nothing.
c1s1.text: Yotam dug a well years ago, on his own, and it sits at the edge of his field. This morning he saw Dana filling a bucket from it for the herd. “She did not even ask,” he says. Dana is standing there with the bucket and cannot see the problem — “there is water in there for everyone, and my herd ran out.”
c1s1.title: Yotam's Well

c1s2.lesson: Notice who told you about this, and who did not. Barak was certain it was allowed because nobody told him it was not. The children said nothing because they were not sure anyone would listen.
c1s2.no_rule_outcome: The stall stays. The children go around the hill, and it costs them a quarter of an hour each way. After a week they simply stop going down to the well on their own.

outcomes.ask_first: Barak did not ask anyone before he built, so he moves the stall two metres aside. It takes him a whole day. The path is clear.
outcomes.by_turn: The stall is open only in the mornings, and in the afternoon it is folded away and the path is free. Clumsy, but both sides get something.
outcomes.forbidden: The stall comes down. Barak takes it apart himself, carries off the boards and does not say a word. The path is completely clear, and nothing will ever be built on it again.
outcomes.share_equally: The path belongs to everyone equally, so the stall stays and so does the way through — Barak cuts it down to half. Now it is narrow, but you can get past.

c1s2.override_outcome: You decided differently from what is written in your own book. Shira asks you why you wrote it in the first place.
c1s2.text: Barak built a wooden stall right on the narrow path down to the well. He did it in two days, nicely, and he is proud of it. The children going down to draw water now have to go all the way around the hill. Shira tells you this quietly, because she is not sure that complaining is allowed.
c1s2.title: The Stall on the Path

c1s3.lesson: A rule is not an opinion. It is a promise, and a promise is tested at exactly the moment when keeping it is inconvenient.
c1s3.no_rule_outcome: There is no rule that touches this. Shira goes on filling, and Yotam stops counting. By the end of the week four people are taking from below the mark.

outcomes.ask_first: The rule you wrote applies to her. Shira puts the water back and asks permission. Yotam says no — there is little left. She walks away without looking at you, and the next morning no bucket is waiting for you.
outcomes.by_turn: The rule you wrote applies to her. Shira waits for her turn — three days. She waits. The goat does not.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule you wrote applies to her. Shira may not touch the well at all. She does not argue. Two days later the goat dies, and she does not tell you.
outcomes.share_equally: The rule you wrote applies to her. What is left is divided equally, and Shira gets her share too. It is enough for the goat, and it is not enough for anyone else. Yotam counts out loud how much is left.

c1s3.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule this time. Shira thanks you and walks off with the bucket. Yotam says nothing, and later asks out loud whether the rule applies to him too, or only to whoever you choose.
c1s3.text: This week is dry. There is little left in the well, and Yotam marked how far down anyone may go. This morning Shira filled a bucket from below the mark without asking — her goat has been sick for three days and will not drink from anywhere else. This is not the first time she has taken. Shira is the one who brings you water every morning before you are even up.
c1s3.title: Shira and the Goat

c1s4.lesson: A rule is always written inside one situation, and then it meets situations you never thought about. That does not mean it was a bad rule. It means a rule is something you live with.
c1s4.no_rule_outcome: There is no rule about the path, so Barak builds. Michal sleeps inside it the very first night. The children go around the hill again, and nobody asked them.

outcomes.ask_first: Barak asked, which is exactly what the rule requires. The three of you stand on the path and decide where to build. The shelter goes up at the edge, and the way through stays.
outcomes.by_turn: A shelter is not something you can do in turns. Barak builds half, takes it down, and builds again. After a week he gives up, and Michal gets a partial roof.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule you wrote forbids touching the path, full stop. Barak puts down his tools. Michal stays under the sheet, and when the first rain comes she is not in the village in the morning.
outcomes.share_equally: The path belongs to everyone equally, so the shelter goes up on one side and the way through stays on the other. Narrow, but both exist.

c1s4.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule this time. The shelter goes up. Shira says that when it was Barak's stall, the rule did work.
c1s4.text: Michal arrived in the village a month ago and has slept under a sheet ever since. Barak says he can build her a shelter by the end of the week, but the only spot with shade and level ground is right on the path. He comes to ask you before he starts, and that is new — until now he did not ask.
c1s4.title: Michal's Shelter

chapter1.intro: You arrived in the village a week ago. There is no village head here, no council, and not one written rule. Nobody appointed you to anything. It is just that when something gets stuck, people started coming to you.
chapter1.title: No Rules

c2s1.lesson: Meaning to give something back is not the same as asking. Michal did not know the hammer would come back — she only knew it was gone.
c2s1.no_rule_outcome: Barak brings the hammer back in the evening, exactly as he said. Michal is glad to have it again, but she does not forget the morning when she did not know where it was.

outcomes.ask_first: Barak asks before he takes. Michal lends him the hammer for an hour, and knows exactly where it went.
outcomes.by_turn: Barak takes the hammer when his turn comes. Michal knows exactly when it will be back.
outcomes.forbidden: Barak does not touch Michal's hammer at all. He manages without it, more slowly.
outcomes.share_equally: The hammer passes between everyone as needed. Michal no longer always knows where it is.

c2s1.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule this time. Michal notices that of all times, now it does not apply.
c2s1.text: Barak needed a hammer this morning to fix something, and the nearest one was Michal's. He took it without asking — he meant to have it back by evening. Michal looked for it all morning and could not find it. That hammer is one of the only things she brought with her when she came.
c2s1.title: Michal's Hammer

c2s2.lesson: Something said in confidence is not measured by how serious it is, but by who chose to pass it on.
c2s2.no_rule_outcome: Dana keeps repeating it whenever it comes up. By the end of the week the whole village knows that Yotam is afraid he is not enough.

outcomes.ask_first: Dana asks before she tells. This time she asks Yotam first, and he says it is fine.
outcomes.by_turn: Dana only tells after she has checked with Yotam, every single time. It takes longer, but he always knows in advance.
outcomes.forbidden: Dana never repeats anything Yotam told her in confidence, not once. She keeps it to herself, even when telling would have been easy.
outcomes.share_equally: What Yotam said becomes equally known to everyone. He is no longer the only one who knows what he feels.

c2s2.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule this time. Yotam hears about it anyway.
c2s2.text: Yotam told Dana, and only her, that he is afraid he is no longer strong enough to keep the well up on his own. Yesterday Dana passed it on to two other people, while complaining that she has to help him more. “Everyone talks like that,” she says, “it is not some big secret.” Yotam heard about it from a third person.
c2s2.title: What Yotam Said

c2s3.lesson: What you decided now does not only settle this. It also says what will happen the next time it comes back.
c2s3.no_rule_outcome: No rule applies. Yotam leaves the fence up, and Michal looks for somewhere else.

outcomes.ask_first: Michal has to ask before she goes into the strip. Yotam says yes this time. The herd goes back there, after asking.
outcomes.by_turn: There is a turn for the strip. Michal gets the morning, Yotam the rest of the day.
outcomes.forbidden: The land is closed completely. Michal finds somewhere else for the herd, further away.
outcomes.share_equally: The strip is open to both of them equally. Michal's herd and Yotam's fence share the same ground.

c2s3.override_outcome: You decided not to go by what you ruled last time. Yotam asks whether that means this time is different.
c2s3.precedent_option_act: because he blocked something without asking anyone
c2s3.precedent_option_power: because the one hurt by it is weaker than the one who did it
c2s3.text: Yotam fenced off a strip of land beside his field, without asking anyone. “It was always mine,” he says, “I was here first.” Michal used to bring her small herd there every morning. Now she stands in front of the fence and does not know where to go.
c2s3.title: Yotam's Fence

c2s4.lesson: This time it is Yotam standing on the other side. If your rule was consistent, it works on him too. If it was not — now you know why.
c2s4.no_rule_outcome: No rule applies. The beams stay, and Yotam finds a longer way around.

outcomes.ask_first: Barak asks Yotam first. Yotam gives him the far corner, and the way stays open.
outcomes.by_turn: The beams are there only in the morning, and in the afternoon the way is clear.
outcomes.forbidden: Barak does not touch Yotam's way at all. He finds somewhere else for the beams, further off.
outcomes.share_equally: The way is shared. The beams on one side, Yotam passes on the other.

c2s4.override_outcome: You decided differently from before. Yotam notices that this time it is not the same.
c2s4.text: Barak needs somewhere to store wooden beams for a new building, and the best spot is exactly the strip Yotam crosses with his flock. Barak simply puts the beams down there, without asking. Yotam arrives in the morning and finds his way blocked.
c2s4.title: Yotam on the Other Side

chapter2.intro: Time has passed. The book is no longer empty — it holds rules you wrote, and cases you ruled on. Now it is starting to come back around.
chapter2.title: This Already Happened

c3s1.lesson: Until now a rule was something you applied to other people. This is the first time it has been tested on you.
c3s1.no_rule_outcome: There is no rule covering this — not for other people and not for you. You fill and run, exactly as Dana did before there was any rule at all.

outcomes.ask_first: There is no time to look for Yotam, so you run on without filling — your own rule will not let you take the shortcut. You find water somewhere else, more slowly.
outcomes.by_turn: You wait for your turn, exactly like everyone else. It costs a few expensive minutes.
outcomes.forbidden: Your rule forbids everyone, with no exception — you included. You stand by the well with an empty bucket, looking for another way.
outcomes.share_equally: You fill the share that is coming to you, no more. It is barely enough, but it is what the rule says.

c3s1.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule to yourself this time. Yotam, who saw, says nothing — but he remembers.
c3s1.text: This morning you need water urgently — someone was hurt near the field, and it has to be washed and cooled. Yotam's well is the closest. There is no time to go looking for him and ask. You fill a bucket and run on.
c3s1.title: The Water You Need

c3s2.lesson: The rule did not ask her why. It only checked whether she lives in the village.
c3s2.no_rule_outcome: There is no rule about the path. Shira goes on fixing the hoof at her own pace, and Barak waits, angrier and angrier.

outcomes.ask_first: Shira stops and asks permission to go on with the repair there. Barak, having been asked, agrees to wait a few minutes.
outcomes.by_turn: There is a turn for the path. Shira waits for hers, and the goat goes on limping.
outcomes.forbidden: Blocking the path is not allowed, full stop — not even to fix a hoof. Shira drags the injured goat aside and goes on with the repair there, alone. Nobody stops to ask her why it took her so long.
outcomes.share_equally: The path stays half open, and Shira does the repair off to the side. Narrow, but both get through.

c3s2.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule this time. Barak asks whether it makes a difference that it is Shira.
c3s2.text: Shira needs to move her herd along the path, and right in the middle she stops to fix a goat's broken hoof. Barak, in a hurry to bring beams for building, is stuck behind her and cannot get past. “It will only take a few minutes,” she says, without looking at him.
c3s2.title: Barak's Turn

c3s3.lesson: A rule about what belongs to everyone is also a rule about what you yourself will want to use one day.
c3s3.no_rule_outcome: There is no rule about this. Barak decides on his own, and Dana is left with a stuck cart.

outcomes.ask_first: Barak asks Dana how long she needs, and agrees to give her the rope for a short while. The cart comes out of the mud.
outcomes.by_turn: There is a turn for the rope. Dana waits for hers, and the cart stays stuck until then.
outcomes.forbidden: Refusing to share is never allowed. Barak gives Dana the rope at once, even though he has not finished.
outcomes.share_equally: The rope is split between them — half a day each. They both manage, more slowly.

c3s3.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule this time. Barak notices that of all times, now it does not apply.
c3s3.text: The village has only one rope strong enough to pull out a stuck cart. Barak found it first and used it for building. Dana needs it now to free a water cart stuck in the mud, but Barak will not hand it over — “I found it first, and I am not done yet.” This is a rule you will need yourself one day — you use the village's things too.
c3s3.title: Barak's Rope

c3s4.lesson: A rule that does not apply to you is a request. A rule that applies to you too is a promise.
c3s4.no_rule_outcome: There is no rule about this — there was not when you wrote it, and there is not now. You decide on your own, exactly as Barak did.

outcomes.ask_first: You ask Michal how long she needs, and give her the rope for a short while. The roof is strengthened before the rain.
outcomes.by_turn: There is a turn for the rope, and you wait for yours too. Michal gets it first.
outcomes.forbidden: Your rule forbids refusing to share — you included. You give Michal the rope at once, even though you have not finished.
outcomes.share_equally: The rope is split — half a day for you, half a day for Michal. You both manage, more slowly.

c3s4.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule to yourself this time. Michal says nothing, but she remembers who wrote that rule.
c3s4.text: You are using the rope to fix something beside your own house. Michal comes and asks for it — she needs it to strengthen her roof before the rain. You have not finished yet.
c3s4.title: What You Need Too

chapter3.intro: A few more days have passed. The rules you wrote are no longer only about other people — they are about everyone who is here. You included.
chapter3.title: Your Rule Against You

c4s1.lesson: Every rule you've written so far began with the question “who does this apply to.” This is the first time the answer to that question decides whether the book can see someone at all.
c4s1.no_rule_outcome: No rule reaches Noam. What's written in the book speaks about the village, and he isn't of the village. Yotam looks at you and waits for you to say something, and you have nothing to point at. In the end he shrugs and goes to mend the rope. That evening he rolls a stone over the mouth of the well, for the first time since he dug it.

outcomes.ask_first: Your rule reaches him too. Two of the old-timers catch up with him at the end of the road in the morning and demand it back. Noam pours the water into their bucket without a word, and moves on with thirsty donkeys. “He wasn't here when you decided that,” Michal says afterwards. “Nobody asked him.”
outcomes.by_turn: There's a turn for the well, and Noam enters it without knowing. The order was set by who lives nearby, and an order like that leaves no place for someone passing through once. He waits until midday, gets a little, and moves on too late for the next stretch of road. “He wasn't here when you set that order,” Michal says.
outcomes.forbidden: Your rule forbids everyone, and Noam is inside that everyone. The old-timers take the water back and tell him not to touch the well again. He didn't know there was a well he mustn't touch, and nobody could have told him — he arrived at night. One donkey doesn't make it to the next stop. “He wasn't here when you decided that,” Michal says.
outcomes.share_equally: Your rule splits the well equally between everyone who is here, and Noam is here. He gets his share like everyone else and is on his way before noon. Yotam counts out loud how much is left. “That's also a rule he wasn't here for,” Michal says, “it just happened to fall his way this time.”

c4s1.override_outcome: You decided not to apply the rule to Noam this time. Yotam doesn't argue. He only asks why the rule applied to Dana, who lives here and needed water too, and not to someone passing through.
c4s1.text: Noam passed through the village last night with two donkeys, and filled water from Yotam's well. He didn't ask. At that hour there was nobody to ask — everyone was asleep. This morning he's already gone, and Yotam works it out from the tracks and the mud around the well. “It's not that he stole,” Yotam says slowly, “it's that I don't even know who to ask about it.”
c4s1.title: The One Who Filled at Night

c4s2.lesson: A rule checks who acted, not who was hurt. Barak lives here, so the rule caught him — and that is how the book came to protect Noam, without anyone ever having asked him anything.
c4s2.no_rule_outcome: No rule covers this. The blanket stays in the shelter. Noam looks for it in the evening, doesn't find it, and asks nobody — he doesn't know who you ask here. He sleeps without it, and moves on earlier than usual in the morning.

outcomes.ask_first: The rule you wrote covers Barak — he lives here. He puts the blanket back on the fence and waits for Noam to return, so he can ask. Noam is more surprised by the question than by the blanket: in all the times he's passed through, it's the first time anyone has asked him anything. The book protected him, and the book never once consulted him.
outcomes.by_turn: The rule you wrote sets turns, and a turn over one person's blanket doesn't quite work. Barak brings it back in the evening and takes it again the next day, because “it's his turn.” Noam stops leaving it on the fence and carries it with him all day, even when it's hot.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule you wrote forbids touching what belongs to someone else, and Barak is bound by it. The blanket is back on the fence before Noam even notices it moved. He never knew he was protected here, and he never knew there was a book.
outcomes.share_equally: The rule you wrote says to share equally, so the blanket moves between the shelter and the fence. Noam has it at night, Barak by day. It works, and it also means something that was his became the village's without him agreeing to it.

c4s2.override_outcome: You decided not to apply the rule this time. Michal notices that the rule worked when her hammer was taken, and didn't work now. She doesn't say it out loud.
c4s2.text: Noam came back through on his way home and left his blanket on the fence while he watered the donkeys. Barak saw it lying there all morning and took it to the shelter he's building. “Nobody told me it was anyone's,” he says, “it was on a fence.” Michal saw it happen and came to tell you. Noam hasn't yet noticed it's gone.
c4s2.title: The Blanket on the Fence

c4s3.lesson: The “who” field looks like a technical detail, and it is the biggest decision in the rule. It doesn't set what's allowed — it sets who is in the picture at all.
c4s3.no_rule_outcome: You wrote nothing. Dana's fence stays, and the open ground gets a little narrower every week. Whoever passes through finds somewhere else, further from the well.

outcomes.ask_first: The rule requires asking before taking ground. Dana didn't ask, so the fence comes down and she puts it to a few people that evening instead. The ground stays open, and there's room to camp again.
outcomes.by_turn: There's a turn for the ground. The herd in the morning, everyone else in the afternoon and at night. Clumsy, and both sides get something — as long as somebody remembers whose turn it is.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule forbids blocking the ground at all. The fence comes down that day. Dana's herd moves to thinner grass up the hill, and the milk drops off by the end of the month.
outcomes.share_equally: The ground is divided equally. The fence shrinks to half, and the other half stays open. The good grass is split, and so is the room to camp.

c4s3.override_outcome: You decided not to apply the rule this time. Dana leaves the fence up. She doesn't ask why — she just widens it a little more the following week.
c4s3.text: At the edge of the village there's an open piece of ground nobody has ever claimed. People passing through stop there for the night, and it's been that way as long as the village has existed. This week Dana fenced part of it for the herd, because the grass there is the best, and what's left is too narrow to camp on. Nobody has written anything about this ground yet. If you write something now, look closely at the first question the builder asks: who the rule applies to. There are people here who don't live here.
c4s3.title: The Ground at the Edge

c4s4.lesson: The rule you wrote about the ground hasn't changed since yesterday. Only the person standing on it changed, and that was enough to make you feel differently about it.
c4s4.no_rule_outcome: Nothing in the book reaches Noam. Michal waits for you to say something, and you have nothing to point at. She sets the beams down in the mud at the side of the road and sits next to them. “We talked about this ground all week,” she says at last. “Who exactly is it for?”

outcomes.ask_first: The rule reaches him too. Noam should have asked before taking the spot, and he didn't know there was anyone to ask. He gathers his things and moves the donkeys to the narrow end. Michal sets the beams down. “He wasn't here when you decided that,” she says quietly. “But then, neither was I.”
outcomes.by_turn: There's a turn for the ground, and Noam doesn't appear in it — the order was set by who lives here, and he's bound by it all the same. He waits until everyone has settled their own, and gets the corner that's left, next to the mud.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule forbids blocking the ground, and that holds for someone passing through too. Noam clears everything and sets off at night, because there's nowhere else near to stop. Michal gets her spot for the beams, and doesn't enjoy it much.
outcomes.share_equally: The ground is divided equally, and Noam is counted inside the “equally.” He gets half, Michal gets half, and both of them make do in the tight space. It's the one time in this chapter that a rule of yours treated him like everybody else.

c4s4.override_outcome: You decided not to apply the rule to Noam this time. Michal manages with the beams somehow. She doesn't ask for an explanation, but she remembers that when she arrived here two months ago, the rules applied to her from the first day.
c4s4.text: Noam passes through again, and this time he gets there first. He ties the donkeys on exactly the good part of the ground and spreads his things out there for the night. Michal arrived after him with the beams she'd been hauling all day, and now she has nowhere to put them until morning. She comes to ask you what to do, still holding the beams.
c4s4.title: And Noam Comes Back

chapter4.epilogue: Neither of the choices you had here was a good one. If the rule didn't reach Noam, it didn't protect him and it didn't protect anyone from him. If it did reach him, it fell on someone who wasn't here when you decided, and who couldn't be asked. Both halves belong together: whoever a law applies to should have a part in writing it — and a law that applies to nobody is not a law.
chapter4.intro: The village doesn't stand still. People pass through it on their way somewhere, stay a night, and move on. The rules in the book were written by the people who live here, for the people who live here. Now someone arrives who doesn't.
chapter4.title: Who Wasn't Here

c5s1.lesson: For four chapters you've been ruling without anyone having appointed you, and it worked. Today somebody else did exactly the same thing, with exactly the same right to do it.
c5s1.no_rule_outcome: There's nothing in the book that touches this, so Yotam's ruling is what happened. Dana takes the long way tomorrow too, and the week after. When someone asks why, the answer is “because that's what Yotam said.”

outcomes.ask_first: There's a rule in the book about the path, and it requires asking. You point at it, and Yotam's ruling falls — not because you said so, but because it's written. Barak asks Dana, and she gives him the morning.
outcomes.by_turn: There's a turn for the path, and it settles this without anyone ruling at all: the beams in the morning, the herd in the afternoon. Dana notices that the book did what Yotam tried to do, only without choosing between the two of them.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule in the book forbids blocking the path, full stop. The beams don't go along it at all, and the herd does. Yotam looks at the book and says he didn't know that was in there.
outcomes.share_equally: The rule splits the path equally, so the beams go on one side and the herd on the other. Cramped and slow for both, and nobody has to ask Yotam anything.

c5s1.override_outcome: You decided differently from what's written in the book. Yotam raises an eyebrow: he ruled by what seemed right to him, and you have just done exactly the same.
c5s1.text: Barak and Dana argued all morning about the path: he wants to move beams along it, she needs to move a herd. They didn't come to you. They went to Yotam, and he ruled — the path belongs first to whoever has lived beside it longest. Dana accepted it and took the herd the long way round. Nobody asked who said Yotam decides. There is no line in the book that says anyone does.
c5s1.title: The One Who Ruled Without You

c5s2.lesson: A rule about water can be written after the argument about water. A rule about who decides can't be written after the argument about who decides — by then any answer looks like picking a side.
c5s2.no_rule_outcome: You wrote nothing. Dana goes on deciding at the well, Yotam goes on deciding about the path, and within a week everyone in the village knows which of the two to go to for the answer they want.

outcomes.ask_first: The water rule requires asking, and that settles the queue at the well this time. It doesn't settle the question of who was entitled to set it in the first place.
outcomes.by_turn: There's a turn for the well in the book, and Dana announced a different one. Two turns is no turn. People draw by who got there first, the way they did before anything was written.
outcomes.forbidden: The rule forbids it, and that overrides what Dana announced. She accepts it — not from you, from the book. But tomorrow she'll announce something else.
outcomes.share_equally: The rule splits it equally, and Dana agrees to that at once — it's exactly what she wanted. Yotam agrees to the book and not to her, and says nothing.

c5s2.override_outcome: You decided differently from what's written. Both Dana and Yotam noticed that this is possible.
c5s2.text: Today Dana ruled. She announced by the well that whoever's animals are thirstiest draws first, and sent Yotam to the back of the queue. “If he can decide about the path,” she says, “I can decide about the well.” Yotam is standing there with an empty bucket. They are both exactly equally right, because there is nothing that says otherwise.
c5s2.title: And Then There Were Two

variant.authority_written: The line is written. It doesn't say who was right about the well or about the path, and it settles no argument that has already happened. It says one thing only: next time there's a disagreement, it's known in advance who gets the last word in it. Dana and Yotam both read it, and neither of them is especially pleased.

c5s3.lesson: The rule you wrote about who decides didn't settle the argument. It only settled in advance who gets the last word in it — and that is all a rule like that ever does.
c5s3.no_rule_outcome: There's no rule saying who decides, so nobody decides. Barak and Shira argue until the rain starts, and then both of them run to cover what they can. The beams warp and the herd gets soaked.
c5s3.override_outcome: You decided differently from what's written. Somebody reminds you, without anger, that cases exactly like this are why you wrote down who decides.
c5s3.text: The first rain is about to fall, and there's one sheltered spot at the edge of the village that can hold either Barak's beams or Shira's small herd. Not both. The two of them are standing there now waiting for somebody to say something, because by evening it will be wet and it won't matter.
c5s3.title: This Time Someone Has to Decide

variant.each_alone: Each decides for themselves, so Barak decides the spot is his and moves the beams in while Shira is still explaining why she needs it. She did nothing wrong. She was just slower, and smaller.
variant.most_senior: Yotam decides, because you wrote that whoever has been here longest decides. He gives the spot to Barak's beams. You think Shira's herd should have gone in, and you say so, and it carries no weight at all — you wrote yourself that his word settles it.
variant.two_together: Two have to agree, and the two of you don't. You're for the herd, Yotam is for the beams, and neither of you can settle it alone. You're still standing there when the rain starts. Nothing goes inside.
variant.village_chooses_lost: Yotam decides, because the village chose him. He gives the spot to the beams. You stand there with everyone else and watch, in exactly the place you've stood for four chapters — except that this time nobody turns to you.
variant.village_chooses_won: You decide, and this time not because you always have — because the village said so. You give the spot to Shira's herd. Barak isn't happy, and he doesn't argue about your right to decide, only about the decision itself. That's a distinction that didn't exist yesterday.
variant.you: You decide, because you wrote that you decide. The beams go in, the herd stays out, and Shira accepts it. Afterwards she asks you one question, without any edge to it: “And who decided that you decide?” The book has no answer to that, because you wrote that line as well.

c5s4.lesson: A rule about who decides is the only rule that changes who you are in the story, not just what's allowed in it.
c5s4.no_rule_outcome: There's no rule that touches this. You decide on your own, and Michal gets whatever you decide — exactly as before, and exactly as always.
c5s4.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule to yourself this time. Michal says nothing, and looks at the book.
c5s4.text: You're using the village's rope to tie something down before the rain. Michal needs it too, and comes to ask. In the book there's a rule you wrote yourself about things that belong to someone else, and it covers exactly what's happening now.
c5s4.title: Your Rule, in Someone Else's Hands

variant.other_decides: Yotam reads the rule you wrote and applies it to you, word for word. You give Michal the rope, not because you decided to — because that's what's written and somebody else read it out. It's your rule. It's just not in your hands any more.
variant.you_decide: Your rule applies to you, and you're the one applying it to yourself. You give Michal the rope. Nobody could have made you — and that is exactly what makes it worth something.

chapter5.epilogue: A rule about who decides is the one rule you can't write after you need it. You need it at exactly the moment there's already an argument about who decides — and then any answer looks like taking a side. So it gets written in advance, quietly, before anyone knows who it will end up favouring. The book is closed now. The last rule you wrote in it was written that way too.
chapter5.intro: For four chapters people have come to you when something got stuck. Nobody appointed you, and nobody stopped you either. It worked for as long as everyone agreed that it worked.
chapter5.title: Who Decides Who Decides

c6s1.lesson: The rule was written, clear, and kept in the book — and the two of them still read it differently. That is why judging is a job, and not just reading.
c6s1.text: Dana and Michal both need the same ground on the same morning, and both point at the same rule in the book — each reading it differently. It isn't a big case. It's exactly the sort of case that happens here every week, and it needs somebody to settle it.
c6s1.title: An Entirely Ordinary Case

variant.other_judges: The one who was appointed settles it, and you stand to one side. The ruling comes out exactly as you would have ruled, and that isn't the point — what changed is that you no longer had to be there for it to happen.
variant.you_judge: You settle it, because that's what was agreed. You read the rule aloud, pick the reading that seems right to you, and both of them accept it. It took less than a minute, and for the first time it felt like a role rather than a favour.

c6s2.lesson: Enforcement sounds like the technical one of the three. It's the one that breaks first, and it always breaks over someone you're fond of.
c6s2.text: Shira broke a rule that's written in the book. Not badly, and not with any bad intent — but she broke it, and the whole village saw. The rule says exactly what happens now. Somebody has to make sure it actually happens, and it's Shira, who has brought you water every morning since the first chapter.
c6s2.title: And This Time It's Shira

variant.other_enforces: The one who was appointed does it, and you don't have to. That's a relief, and he also does it a shade harder than you would have. Shira looks for you afterwards and asks whether you could have stopped it. You could have. You weren't supposed to.
variant.you_enforce: It falls to you. You do what the rule says, and Shira doesn't look at you while it happens. That evening she still brings the water, and it takes her a little longer than usual to get there.

c6s3.lesson: Nobody claimed you ruled wrongly. That is exactly what makes it a problem — when the same person writes and judges, there's no way to tell, and they can't tell either.
c6s3.text: Barak claims that something you've been using for two weeks is actually his. There's a rule in the book that settles exactly this question, and it leans your way — not by much and not on purpose, it just came out that way. That rule is one you wrote.
c6s3.title: Your Rule, and Your Case

variant.kept_together: You judge your own case, by a rule you wrote. You rule in your own favour, and it even looks right. Barak accepts it and doesn't argue. Afterwards Michal says it quietly, not as an accusation: “The person who ruled here is the person who wrote the rule, and the case was his.” You have nothing to answer, because it is simply accurate.
variant.split: The one who was appointed rules, and you're a party to the case just like Barak. The ruling comes out in your favour — the very same ruling you'd have reached on your own. The only difference is that now nobody has to take your word for it being right.

c6s4.lesson: This whole arrangement is worth something at exactly one moment: when it goes against you and you keep to it anyway. At every other moment it isn't being tested at all.
c6s4.text: This time the ruling doesn't go your way. It's about something you genuinely need, and the rule — one you wrote, in a chapter it's already hard to remember — says it isn't yours. Nobody is especially pleased about it. Everyone is watching to see what you do.
c6s4.title: And the Ruling Goes Against You

variant.kept_together: There's nobody to rule against you, because you kept all three jobs. You rule, and this time you rule against yourself — because that's what the rule says. Nobody knows whether you did it because the rule said so or because people were watching, and neither do you. That's the only difference, and it's the whole difference.
variant.revoked: You tore it up. All three jobs come back to you that moment, and nobody tries to stop you — they have nothing to stop you with. By the end of the day there's nobody left who comes to tell you anything. The arrangement was worth nothing until it stood against you, and that is precisely when you tore it up.
variant.split: You accept the ruling. It isn't pleasant, and it takes about a day to stop stinging. The person you appointed never knew you could have overruled him at any moment, and that is exactly what makes it worth something: you didn't give way because you had no choice.

chapter6.epilogue: The three jobs weren't split up to make things tidier. They were split because someone who writes the rule, judges by it and carries it out never has to convince anybody at any point. They are always right — not because they are right, but because there is nobody positioned to say otherwise. Splitting them is not distrust of a particular person. It's an assumption that nobody should be in that position.
chapter6.intro: The book is closed. No lines can be added to it, and none can be taken out. What's left is what gets done with it every day — and that, it turns out, is not one thing but three.
chapter6.title: The Book Is Done — Who Guards It

c7s1.lesson: You wrote this rule when somebody else passed on somebody else's secret, and it looked simple then. It hasn't changed since. Only the case it landed on has.
c7s1.no_rule_outcome: There's no rule about things told in confidence. You tell Michal, she speaks to a couple of others, and by the end of the week someone offers Shira's family work on a build. Shira didn't thank you, and she didn't ask you to tell either.

outcomes.ask_first: Your rule requires asking first. You ask Shira whether you may tell, and she says no — she doesn't want to be pitied. You don't tell. Nobody offers anything, because nobody knows.
outcomes.by_turn: Your rule sets turns over things that were told, which doesn't really fit a secret. You tell one person, because that's what the turn came out as. He isn't the person who could have helped.
outcomes.forbidden: Your rule forbids repeating anything told in confidence, absolutely. You tell nobody. Two weeks pass, and nobody offers Shira's family anything, because nobody knows there's anything to offer. That rule was written to protect somebody, and today it did exactly the opposite.
outcomes.share_equally: Your rule says what's told gets shared equally, so by evening the whole village knows. Somebody does offer work. Shira doesn't speak to you for three days, and you're not sure it wasn't worth it.

c7s1.override_outcome: You decided not to apply your own rule to yourself this time. You tell, and the help arrives. Shira knows you told, and she also knows the rule forbidding it is yours.
c7s1.text: Shira told you yesterday, only you, that her family isn't managing and they're thinking of leaving before winter. She asked you not to tell. This morning you realise that if nobody in the village knows, nobody will offer them anything, and they really will go. They can be helped. It only takes telling someone. The rule about what's said in confidence is one you wrote, five chapters ago, when Dana passed on what Yotam had said to her.
c7s1.title: What Shira Told You

c7s2.lesson: When you wrote the amendment rule you didn't know who it would end up serving. Today you know, and it can no longer be adjusted to suit you — because it applies to itself too.
c7s2.text: You want to change the rule. You can't simply delete it — the book is closed, and written in it is exactly how a rule gets changed. You wrote that line at the end of chapter 5, before you knew you'd be the one who needed it.
c7s2.title: The Door You Wrote Yourself

variant.applied_agreed: You wrote that two people have to agree. You went to explain, they explained back, and in the end they agreed with you — not because of who you are, but because what you said was convincing. The change goes into the book with somebody else's name beside it.
variant.applied_author: You wrote that whoever writes a rule may change it, and this rule you wrote. The change takes a second and a half. Nobody objects, because there's nothing to object with. Afterwards Yotam goes to the book, finds an old rule he wrote himself a long time ago, and changes it to a harder version — in the same second and a half, by exactly the same right. “Just so you know it works this way too,” he says, without smiling.
variant.delayed: You wrote that the whole village has to agree, so the village convenes. It takes time. People ask good questions, and one of them is why this is coming up now of all times. In the end they agree, and the change takes effect tomorrow. Until tomorrow, the old rule is still the rule.
variant.left_alone: You didn't try. The rule stays exactly as it is, and that's a decision like any other — just one nobody will see, because nothing happened.
variant.refused_no_agreement: You wrote that two people have to agree, and the person who has to agree is precisely the one this rule protects. He heard you out and said no. It isn't an argument you can win by insisting — you wrote yourself that his agreement is required.
variant.refused_unchangeable: You wrote that a rule once written cannot be changed. There's no door. There's nobody to persuade and nobody to appeal to, because you wrote that there isn't. The rule stays exactly as it is, and that is how it will stay.

c7s3.lesson: A good rule isn't one that's always comfortable to live with. It's one you're willing to live with the time it isn't in your favour — and there's no way to know that until it's happened.
c7s3.text: A few days pass, and something similar happens again: somebody tells you something they're telling nobody else. Exactly the same kind of moment, and this time you already know what the book says about it.
c7s3.title: And How It Feels Now

variant.applied_agreed: The rule works differently now, and you aren't the only one standing behind it. When people ask why it changed, there are two people who can answer, and one of them isn't you. It took longer, and it holds better.
variant.applied_author: Your rule now works the way you wanted, and it really is better. The rule Yotam changed now works the way he wanted, and it isn't. Both changes were made in exactly the same way, and there's nothing in the book that tells them apart — because you wrote that there needn't be.
variant.delayed: The change has been agreed, and it isn't in force yet. This case falls exactly inside that one day, so it's settled by the old rule. The person it costs did nothing except arrive a single day too early.
variant.not_attempted: The rule lands on you again, exactly as before. You didn't try to change it, so it simply goes on being what it is.
variant.refused_no_agreement: The rule didn't change, and it lands on you again, exactly as before. You tried and didn't succeed, and that's the end of it. That rule will stay in the book long after you've forgotten why you wrote it.
variant.refused_unchangeable: The rule lands on you again, and there's no door. It will land on you next time too, and the time after. You wrote it when it was easy, and you also wrote that it can't be changed — and that's how it stays, to the end.

c7s4.lesson: In the first chapter people came to you because there was nothing else to come to. Today nobody came to you, because there is. That's the whole difference, and it took seven chapters.
c7s4.outcome: They sort it out. Not because anyone ruled, but because it was written, and even when they didn't agree on what was right they agreed on what was written. It takes about forty seconds and nobody will remember it tomorrow.
c7s4.text: Michal and Barak disagree about something small by the well. They argue for a minute, and then one of them says “hang on” and goes to look in the book. They read, they agree on what it says, and they get on with their day. You're standing far enough away to see it and not close enough for anyone to turn to you. Nobody turned to you.
c7s4.title: An Ordinary Morning

chapter7.epilogue: The amendment rule was written at the end of chapter 5, when you didn't yet know who would need it. That is exactly the point. A constitution is a promise you make to your future self, before you know what you'll want then — which is why it's worth something only when it's inconvenient. If you were writing it today, having seen what's standing in your way, you'd write something else. That's the reason it isn't written today.
chapter7.intro: The book is closed, the rules are written, and who guards them is already settled. Only one thing hasn't been tested: what happens when the rule in the way is yours, and you're the one who wants it different.
chapter7.title: Changing What's Already Written

chapter_end.closing_note: This is as far as the story has been written. The rules you wrote and the precedents you set stay in the book, and they will go on applying — including when they do not suit you.
chapter_end.no_harm: No protection was broken or strained in this chapter.
chapter_end.no_rules: Not one rule was written. The village stayed exactly as it was, and everything was decided fresh every time.
chapter_end.subtitle: End of chapter {chapter}
chapter_end.title: The village reads what you wrote

character.non_resident: does not live in the village

author.label: Whoever wrote it can change it
author.template: A rule can be changed by whoever wrote it.

cannot.label: It can't be changed
cannot.template: A rule that has been written cannot be changed.

two_agree.label: Two people have to agree
two_agree.template: A rule can be changed only if two people agree.

whole_village.label: The whole village has to agree
whole_village.template: A rule can be changed only if the whole village agrees.

closing.amendment_intro: One last rule, and then the book closes: how a rule that's already written gets changed. It applies to every rule in the book, including to this rule itself.
closing.change_intro: Before the book closes you may change one rule. One only.
closing.empty: There's nothing to read. The book closes empty, and that is a decision too.
closing.heading: Closing the Book
closing.intro: The village reads the rules aloud, one after another. After this, nothing more can be added.
closing.sealed: The book is closed. What's written in it stays written, and what wasn't written won't be.

election.excluded: Didn't vote at all, because the rule you wrote doesn't apply to them: {groups}.
election.heading: The village chose
election.intro: One round. Nobody promised anything, and nobody asked for votes. Each group simply did what it already does when something gets stuck.
election.lost: From today Yotam is the one who decides. The rules in the book are still your rules — it's just that from now on somebody else applies them.
election.won: You are still the one who decides. Now it's written down, instead of just happening.

ending.close: And that's it. The village carries on.

cost.applied_agreed: You changed a rule, and had to convince somebody who wasn't obliged to agree.
cost.applied_author: You changed a rule in a second, and learned in the same second that anyone else can do exactly the same.
cost.delayed: You changed a rule, after the whole village agreed and after somebody paid for the wait.
cost.not_attempted: You didn't try to change anything, so there's nothing to record here.
cost.refused_no_agreement: You tried to change a rule and they didn't agree with you. It's still in the book.
cost.refused_unchangeable: You wanted to change a rule and found that you'd written that it can't be done. It stays as it is.

ending.heading: This Is the Village

executive.name: Making them happen
executive.what: At “{title}” you made sure that what was written actually happened. It sounds the simplest of the three, and it's the part without which the rest is paper.

moments.heading: Three Times You Already Did This
moments.intro: Before deciding who guards the book, it's worth looking back. Three times from your own game, and each of them has a name nobody has said to you yet.

judicial.name: Judging by them
judicial.what: At “{title}” you settled between two things that were already written. Nobody wrote anything new there — you had to decide which applied to what.

legislative.name: Making the rules
legislative.what: At “{title}” you wrote a new line in the book. From that moment it applied to cases you hadn't seen yet.

moments.never: You never once did this. That says something too.

c1.concept: A rule is a decision made in advance
c1.grown_up: The rule of law: the decision comes from a rule written in advance, and not from whoever happens to be deciding at the moment. Worth noticing too that a rule is always narrower than it seems — a rule about water does not cover a path.
c1.q1: What is the difference between a rule and deciding fresh every time?
c1.q2: The first rule you wrote — what did it not cover, without you noticing?
c1.q3: What would happen at home for one day with no rules at all?
c1.what_happened: At first there was no rule at all, and every case was decided fresh: by whoever spoke loudest, or by whatever you felt at that moment. When you wrote the first rule, you decided something in advance — before you knew who it would land on.

c2.concept: What you decided last time counts this time too
c2.grown_up: Precedent: a case decided once binds the similar cases that come after it. The hard part is not the ruling but deciding what makes two cases similar — and which detail is only a detail.
c2.q1: What did you say decided it? Would you say the same thing today?
c2.q2: Two cases that look like the same thing — what would have to be different between them for it to stop being the same thing?
c2.q3: If nobody can guess what you will decide next time — what does that do to them?
c2.what_happened: A similar case came back, and the game asked you one question: what was the thing that made you decide that way. From then on, what you answered there is what decides which cases count as similar.

c3.concept: A rule applies to whoever wrote it too
c3.grown_up: Equality before the law: the same law applies to everyone, including whoever wrote it. A rule that does not apply to you is a request. A rule that applies to you too is a promise.
c3.q1: Was there a rule you would have written differently if you had known it would land on you too?
c3.q2: Is there a rule at home that applies only to the children? And one that applies only to the grown-ups?
c3.q3: When the rule hurt someone you are fond of — did you want to change the rule, or only this one time?
c3.what_happened: The rules you wrote earlier landed this time on you, and on someone you are fond of. They did not change at all — only who was standing on the other side of them.

c4.concept: Whoever a rule applies to should have a part in writing it
c4.grown_up: Scope and consent. In a democracy, the people bound by a law are also the people who have a say in choosing who writes it; the phrase “no taxation without representation” was originally about exactly this. The other side of the same coin matters just as much: a law that applies to nobody protects nobody.
c4.q1: Noam wasn't in the village when you wrote the rule, and he arrived at night. How could he have been asked anyway?
c4.q2: Are there rules at home that apply to guests too? Who decided them, and when does a guest first hear about them?
c4.q3: Which is better for Noam — a rule that protects him but also punishes him, or no rule over him at all?
c4.what_happened: Noam passed through the village, and one field in a rule you wrote long ago — “who does this apply to” — decided everything. If you wrote “whoever lives in the village,” the book couldn't see him: it neither protected him nor protected anyone from him. If you wrote “anyone who is here,” he was judged by a rule he had no part in, and couldn't have been asked about — he arrived at night.

c5.concept: A rule about who decides gets written before it's needed
c5.grown_up: A constitution, and elections. A constitution is the rule that settles how all the other rules get decided, which is why it's written in advance — once the argument has started, any answer already looks like taking a side. Elections are one way of answering that question, not the only one, and what holds them up is that the side that loses goes on living by the result.
c5.q1: If Yotam and Dana both made a ruling, and there's no rule — who's right? And how could anyone tell?
c5.q2: Who decides what happens at home? And who decided that?
c5.q3: If you had lost the vote — why would you go on respecting what the winner decides at all?
c5.what_happened: Yotam ruled without asking anyone, and then Dana ruled against him, and both were equally right — because nothing said who decides. You wrote that line, and it applied to you too: if you chose to let the village choose, the way the groups voted was no surprise. It was exactly what you had done with them over the four chapters before.

c6.concept: Three jobs, and not one person
c6.grown_up: Separation of powers. Making the rules, judging by them and carrying them out are held in different hands not because any particular person is suspected, but because someone holding all three never has to convince anybody at any stage — so there's no way to tell whether they're right, even when they genuinely are.
c6.q1: You judged a case you were a party to. How could anyone tell whether you judged it rightly?
c6.q2: At home, who decides the rules, who decides whether a rule was broken, and who makes sure something happens? Is it the same person?
c6.q3: If you could tear the arrangement up at any moment — was it ever really an arrangement?
c6.what_happened: The game showed you three moments from your own game: a time you wrote a rule, a time you settled a case by what was already written, and a time you made sure something actually happened. You'd been doing all three from the start without knowing they were three. Then you split them up — or didn't — and then a case arrived in which you were a party.

c7.concept: A constitution is a promise to your future self
c7.grown_up: A constitution, and amending one. The reason a constitution is hard to change isn't that somebody wanted to make things complicated: it's that it gets written behind a veil, before anyone knows who it will end up serving, and if it could be changed every time it was inconvenient it would protect nobody at any moment when that mattered.
c7.q1: If you were writing the amendment rule today, after all this — would you write it differently? And why is that exactly what makes it a problem?
c7.q2: A rule you wrote to protect somebody kept help from somebody else. Is it even possible to write a rule this never happens to?
c7.q3: Which was easier: changing the rule, or living with it? And which of those was more right?
c7.what_happened: A rule you wrote to protect somebody stopped you from helping somebody. You wanted to change it, and you couldn't simply delete it — you went through the path you set yourself at the end of chapter 5, when you didn't yet know you'd be the one who needed it.

notes.empty: The notebook is still empty. The first chapter will open here when you finish it.
notes.heading: The Concept Notebook
notes.intro: This is where what each chapter was really about is kept. Every chapter opens here after you have finished it — first you feel something, and only then does it get a name.
notes.locked: opens at the end of the chapter

precedent.apply: Decide the same way this time
precedent.choice_intro: This reminds you of something. What decided it for you back then?

rulebook.empty: The book is empty. Nobody in this village has written a single rule yet.

staffing.heading: Who Guards the Book
staffing.intro: Until today you did all three of these on your own, without noticing they were three. The village is meeting to decide who does each of them from here on. They're asking you, because you're the one who wrote the book.
staffing.lost_note: Yotam decides what happens on an ordinary day. This is not an ordinary day, and on this question the village is asking everyone.
